target.title: Archive digitization deadline
target.frame: A local museum is digitizing 4,000 catalog folders before a public exhibition in ten weeks. Scanning is ahead of plan, but metadata review and rights checks have accumulated a backlog. Folders vary greatly in size and completeness, and volunteers work different days. The project lead needs to decide the next two weeks of assignments and whether to revise the promised exhibition scope, using daily counts and a limited sample of folder histories.

instrument.state: Material associated with a past event may persist as a latent residue that ordinary visual inspection does not reveal.
instrument.operation: Apply a probe whose reaction is promoted by material associated with the suspected residue.
instrument.signal: Responsive material produces an otherwise absent, localized observable reaction.
instrument.inference: The reaction supports the presence and location of material capable of producing that response.
instrument.limit: Unrelated substances may produce the same response, relevant residue may fail to respond because it was removed, degraded, or is below detection, and detecting responsive material does not by itself establish the event that produced it. The probe may also alter material needed for later analysis.

mapping.state: Act on folder records and handoff histories, where unresolved metadata questions, rights requests, or failed transfers may leave traces that scanning totals do not reveal. These traces are possible diagnostic residues, not established causes of the reported backlog. Assume folders can be linked across stages by identifier; verify this before interpreting counts. Treat exhibition readiness as requiring the museum’s agreed metadata and rights evidence, which must first be specified.
mapping.operation: Apply an evidence-reconciliation probe: for each sampled folder, compare its recorded stage with dated review decisions, outstanding questions, rights evidence, and handoff acknowledgments. Ask the relevant reviewer to resolve each discrepancy against those records; unresolved traces trigger a localized flag identifying the folder, stage, missing evidence, and next action. Propose a budget of 20 randomly selected histories, distributed across recorded stages and available size, completeness, and queue-age groups; record selection probabilities and unavailable histories. Examine up to five additional suspicious histories separately without using them to estimate prevalence. Each day, reconcile stage arrivals, completions, returns, and remaining queues, alongside actual volunteer hours. Preserve original histories and log probe-generated changes separately. Stop examining a history when its evidence is reconciled or a predefined time allowance expires; label expired or inaccessible cases inconclusive. If identifiers or stage definitions cannot be reconciled, repair that measurement problem before projecting completion.
mapping.signal: Observe whether reconciliation produces a flag that routine totals lacked: for example, a recorded review completion without the required decision, an unanswered rights request, or a transfer without acknowledgment. These are proposed signal types, not observed findings. Record each flag’s location, supporting trace, age, and disposition; distinguish confirmed unresolved work, explained discrepancies, and inconclusive cases. Also observe daily queue changes, rework, and completion per staffed hour within comparable folder groups. A probe-triggered resolution is an intervention and must be recorded separately from evidence of the prior state.
mapping.inference: A supported flag warrants concluding that the specified folder contains evidence of unresolved or inconsistently recorded work at that location. It does not establish why the delay occurred. Use recurring supported flags, queue growth, and measured effort to propose the next two weeks of assignments: allocate suitably trained volunteers to the demonstrated metadata or rights constraint, assign owners to external dependencies, and limit additional scanning where it only increases waiting inventory. Respect actual volunteer availability and required rights authority. Produce a range of ten-week readiness estimates using stage-specific throughput, folder mix, remaining work, and scheduled hours; use only the probability sample for prevalence estimates, with appropriate weighting and uncertainty. Reassess assignments after one week. If even the optimistic supported estimate falls below the promised scope, propose reducing or changing that scope promptly. If the estimate range crosses the promise, identify a contingent reduced scope and gather targeted evidence before the week-two decision. Count only folders meeting the agreed readiness criteria toward the exhibition.
mapping.limit: Legitimate holds, stale status fields, duplicate records, or undocumented completed work may produce the same flags as unresolved work. Missing, overwritten, sparse, or inaccessible histories may conceal relevant traces, so no flag does not establish readiness. A limited sample may miss rare, difficult folders; aggregate counts can conceal size differences, and scanning rates cannot substitute for metadata or rights capacity. Throughput projections remain conditional on staffing, folder mix, rework, and external rights responses; widen ranges or withhold a defensible scope forecast when these inputs are inadequate. Flags do not establish negligence, the original delaying event, or legal clearance. Reconciliation may consume scarce reviewer time, prompt work, or alter records needed for later diagnosis. Retain dated snapshots, cap probe effort, and refer unresolved rights decisions to an authorized decision-maker before inclusion.
